title: The direct path
hook: a direct path for the purification of beings: four foundations of mindfulness (MN 10)

segments.voice: Yesterday: your immeasurables, all four rooms in one sitting. Your line was immeasurable. Day two hundred forty-six, and a new part of the path.

Mindfulness is everywhere now: on apps, in office trainings, on the side of a tea box. Some of it traces back, one way or another, to an old text: a talk the Buddha is said to have given to the people of Kuru, in a market town called Kammasadhamma. For the next three weeks, you'll walk through it, section by section. It's long, and it repeats itself on purpose. Today: the opening line, and the map.
screen: `MINDFULNESS, ON A TEA BOX.` → `ONE OLD TEXT.` → `THREE WEEKS, SECTION BY SECTION.`

segments.voice: The text is the Satipatthana Sutta, number ten in the Middle Length Discourses, with a longer twin, the Maha-satipatthana, in the Long Discourses. Sati means mindfulness, remembering to be present. Patthana is usually taken as foundation or establishing, though scholars argue about how to split the word. So: the establishing of mindfulness. It opens with a bold claim. This, the Buddha says, is the ekayana path, for the purification of beings, for getting past sorrow and lamentation, for the ending of pain and grief, for finding the true way, for realizing nibbana. Ekayana is a puzzle. Some older English translations said the only way. Others say the direct path, or the one-way path, a road that goes straight to one place. The word can bear several meanings, and teachers disagree. Then the map: four foundations, four places to set mindfulness down. The body. Feelings, meaning the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of experience. The mind, its states and moods. And dhammas, a hard word here, often translated mental qualities or phenomena: the patterns the Buddha taught people to recognize. One path, four doors into it. Every section that follows fits somewhere on this map, so when you get lost in the next three weeks, come back to these four.
screen: `SATI + PATTHANA: ESTABLISHING MINDFULNESS.` · `EKAYANA: ONLY, OR DIRECT?` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `ONE PATH, FOUR DOORS.` · then, large: `ONE WAY, FOUR DOORS.`

segments.voice: Touch each door once: body, the weight and contact where you sit; feelings, whether this moment is pleasant, unpleasant or neither; mind, the mood right now, calm, restless, tired. Dhammas: is anything pulling at you, a want, an irritation, a doubt? Name the four quietly, body, feelings, mind, dhammas, and then just sit with the breath.
Satipatthana. The establishing of mindfulness, set down in four places: body, feelings, mind and dhammas.
Your line: one way, four doors. Body, feelings, mind and dhammas, one map. Day two hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: The Satipatthana Sutta is studied and practiced across the Buddhist world, especially in Theravada communities, where many meditation methods, including the Burmese insight traditions, trace themselves to it; the longer version is sometimes chanted in full.

original.note: Pali satipaṭṭhāna: the establishing, or foundation, of mindfulness.

trapdoor: what you thought: satipatthana is just a long word for mindfulness.
what it means: mindfulness set down in four places: body, feelings, mind, dhammas.
what a scholar hears: the compound can split as sati + paṭṭhāna (foundation) or sati + upaṭṭhāna (establishing, being present); commentators and modern scholars read it both ways.
